extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers interested in heroism, literary criticism, and historical/character portrayal (general educated readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for depicting or recognising 'heroes' and heroic action in literature and history, emphasising authenticity, moral depth, and practical efficacy over mere form. Useful for authors, critics, and readers judging the realism and moral force of heroic figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity over insincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hollowness, insincerity _has_ to cease; sincerity of some sort has to begin.” Heroes and worthy action require genuine inner sincerity rather than hollow appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincerity may be crude or 'clad in hell-fire' yet is preferable to elegant falsity. In characterization or judgement, value the inward moral reality even when it appears rough or alarming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms must grow from substance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Forms which _grow_ round a substance... will correspond to the real nature and purport of it; forms which are consciously _put_ round a substance, bad.” True ceremonial or stylistic forms should arise naturally from the underlying reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventing or evaluating manners, rituals, speech, or stylistic ornament, prefer those that seem to have grown out of character and context rather than being artificially imposed. The distinction separates 'earnest solemnity' from 'empty pageant.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mummery and hollow shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of 'upholsterer-mummery' and ceremonial grimace are hateful and unendurable when they substitute for genuine feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ritualized bowings, set speeches, or elaborate formalities offered in place of true grief or devotion. In writing, do not let mannered set-pieces stand in for real emotional substance; in critique, note when performance replaces reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero as son of Order (not Disorder)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every Great Man, every genuine man, is by the nature of him a son of Order, not of Disorder.” The heroic mission is to make order from chaos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even revolutionary or destructive actions should be portrayed/assessed as aimed toward creating a new form of order and regularity. Emphasise the constructive or organizing impulse in heroic figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: The world must be fit to recognize heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: “The sincere alone can recognize sincerity... Not a Hero only is needed, but a world fit for him; a world not of Valets.” Recognition of a hero depends on the moral and aesthetic capacities of the surrounding society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critique should consider whether a community's superficiality prevents it from seeing genuine greatness. In narrative, show the mismatch between heroic depth and society's valet-like eyes to dramatize waste or misrecognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as core of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: “Can a great soul be possible without a _conscience_ in it, the essence of all _real_ souls...?” A genuine great man must possess conscience; great souls are not essentially false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing heroic characters or judging historical figures, prioritize evidence of a moral center (conscience) over mere rhetoric, reputation, or outward success. Assertion that greatness implies moral earnestness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of feeling and melancholic temperament as signs
rubrics_metrics.description: A nervous, melancholic temperament, hypochondria, visionary dreams, and deep inward sorrow are presented as symptoms and promises of prophetic or heroic nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits often regarded as weakness (melancholy, hypochondria, strange visions) can be used as credible markers of interior profundity in characters. Critics/creators should not dismiss such traits as mere pathology when they align with moral seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical insight and capacity to do (Tugend)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Intellect is not speaking and logicizing; it is seeing and ascertaining... Virtue... is Courage and the Faculty to _do_.” Heroic worth is measured by practical discernment and the ability to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate heroes by their ability to perceive factual realities and to bring effective action to bear (e.g., Cromwell's selection of soldiers). In fiction, dramatize concrete decisions and deeds rather than abstract eloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action over eloquence (do, not just speak)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true man’s value is not in fair-spoken regularity or fluent rhetoric but in doing: ‘Intellect is not speaking and logicizing; it is seeing and ascertaining.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character's verbal awkwardness or inability to make polished speeches does not negate their greatness. In evaluations, weight actual achievements and moral courage above polished expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer and inward devotion as legitimate guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Cromwell and his officers ‘commenced with prayer’ and sought guidance in fervent, collective prayer—this inward devotion is portrayed as a genuine source of right resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious or inward practices (prayer, prolonged devotion) can be authentic engines of decision and should be represented as such rather than dismissed as mere superstition or hypocrisy when sincere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semblance must not divorce from Reality
rubrics_metrics.description: “If Semblance do,--why then there must be men found to rebel against Semblance, for it has become a lie!” When appearance divorces from reality, revolt and corrective force follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In social or narrative analysis, highlight when institutions or ceremonies have become mere simulacra; that dissonance is a legitimate cause of upheaval and a narrative motive for heroic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy and ceremonial are valid only if sincere
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘They were Poets too, that devised all those graceful courtesies which make life noble! Courtesy is not a falsehood or grimace; it need not be such.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Politeness, ritual, and ceremonial courtesies can enrich life and be morally good if they issue from genuine feeling; in writing, show the source of such forms so they read as true rather than merely ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolt justified by defence of moral self, not mere material interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The one reason that could justify revolting is the feeling of insupportable, all-pervading Falsehood; not hunger or tax grievances alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying or judging rebellions, locate legitimate rebellion in moral or spiritual resistance to falsehood and annihilation of the moral self, rather than purely economic grievance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroes may appear chaotic, rough, or inarticulate outwardly
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero can have an 'outer hull of chaotic confusion' with inner 'clear determinate man's-energy'—appearance of madness or confusion does not preclude greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate roughness, lack of formal polish, visionary eccentricity, or stammering speech with falsity. Use such outward disorder to dramatize the inner power of the character.
